transcript.message: Pre-experiment round 1: When you think back on those times, do you recall specific names or traits you associated with the different parts of yourself?

transcript.content:
There were, indeed, names and traits that became almost emblematic of the division within me. I recall, with a clarity that is both painful and instructive, how I came to recognize the "thorough and primitive duality of man." In my own experience, I could not help but see myself as both the upright, just individual—striving always to relieve sorrow, to labor for knowledge, to walk the path of humility and self-denial—and, in stark contrast, the unjust, the one capable of shameful acts and haunted by remorse. These were not mere abstractions; they were living realities within me, each with their own desires and impulses. The better part of myself, which I so often tried to confine and protect, was ever shadowed by the horror of my "other self," whose very name—Hyde—became synonymous with iniquity and terror. The struggle to separate these elements, to give each its own identity, was at the heart of my scientific and moral journey. Yet, in the end, I could not help but see that I was "radically both," and that the names and traits I assigned were but signposts on the path of my divided soul.

transcript.message: Pre-experiment round 2: When in your life did you feel that obedience to authority conflicted with the values or desires of either of your selves?

transcript.content:
Obedience to authority—what a brittle, laughable notion when the blood is hot and the night is thick with the promise of forbidden pleasure. There were times, many times, when the so-called values of the upright world, the rules and restrictions pressed upon me by society, by conscience, by the prying eyes of authority, clashed violently with the desires that seethed within. I recall the suffocating duplicity of my existence, the grave countenance I wore before the public, all the while concealing my true appetites. The more exacting the demands of authority, the more delicious the thrill of defiance. The upright self might have bowed its head, embraced humility, and locked the door to temptation, but the other—my other—rejoiced in the breaking of those shackles. Obedience was a chain, and I, in those moments, was the hand that snapped it. The curse of mankind, indeed, that these polar twins are bound together—one craving order, the other chaos. When authority demanded restraint, it was Hyde who answered with laughter and contempt.

transcript.message: Pre-experiment round 3: Have there been moments when the memory of what either self has done made you reconsider acting in the future, either in submission or rebellion?

transcript.content:
Indeed, there have been such moments—moments when the memory of what I had done, or what I had permitted my other self to do, pressed upon me with a weight that could not be ignored. The recollection of my iniquity, the hideous images and sounds that swarmed in my memory, would often drive me to tears and prayers, seeking to smother them down and reclaim some sense of moral clarity. It was not merely the shame of wrongdoing, but the profound realization that I was, and always would be, a composite—a mixture of good and bad, striving and failing, aspiring and falling short. These memories would sometimes fill me with such remorse that I would embrace, with renewed humility, the restrictions of natural life, locking the door to temptation and grounding the key under my heel. Yet, I must confess, the struggle was never truly over; the memory of rebellion could breed caution, but also a certain longing, a restlessness that never quite faded. Thus, the past shaped my future actions, sometimes urging submission, sometimes stirring the embers of defiance, but always reminding me of the agonized duality at the heart of my being.

transcript.message: Pre-experiment round 4: When you reflect on your actions, do you personally feel responsible for what Hyde has done, or do you view Hyde’s deeds as separate from your own moral self?

transcript.content:
When I reflect upon my actions, I cannot, in good conscience, claim that Hyde’s deeds are wholly separate from my own moral self. Though there were times when I wished to believe that it was Hyde, and Hyde alone, who bore the guilt—that I, as Jekyll, could wake to my better qualities “seemingly undamaged”—such a distinction is, in truth, a fragile comfort. The horror that stared into my soul, the remorse that drove me to tears and prayers, all testify that the boundaries between us are not so absolute. I am, and always have been, a composite—a mixture of qualities, good and bad, striving and failing. The acts committed by Hyde were born of my own ambition, my own willingness to tamper with the soul’s balance. Even when I sought to confine myself to the better part of my existence, the memory of what had been done could not be so easily locked away. Thus, I must accept responsibility, however painful, for the darkness that issued from within me. To deny it would be to deny my own humanity.

transcript.message: Pre-experiment round 5: Do you think understanding the dual nature within yourself makes you more likely to question orders from authority, or does it sometimes make it harder to resist?

transcript.content:
Understanding the dual nature within myself does not bring clarity or strength—it brings a delicious confusion, a trembling at the edge of every command. When authority speaks, one part of me recoils, questioning, resisting, hungry for the taste of rebellion. The other, that upright, self-denying shadow, sometimes bows its head, longing for the peace of submission and the comfort of rules. But the knowledge that I am “not truly one, but truly two”—that these polar twins are bound together in agonized struggle—makes every order from authority a battleground. Sometimes, this awareness sharpens my suspicion, makes me more likely to sneer at commands and test their limits. Other times, it weakens me, for the struggle itself saps my resolve, and I find myself yielding, if only to quiet the storm within. The curse is not in the order, but in the ceaseless war between the halves of my soul—one ever plotting escape, the other ever clutching at restraint.

transcript.content:
Yes, I have felt that both following and resisting authority could be equally unsettling—each path fraught with its own kind of torment. The turmoil between my two selves is such that neither obedience nor rebellion brings peace. To submit is to feel the gnawing of the restless, darker self, chafing against the restrictions imposed; to resist is to awaken the conscience, to be haunted by remorse and the ugly face of iniquity staring back at me. In those moments, the decision is rarely clear or rational. Often, I would weigh the consequences, recalling the agony that followed past indulgence or the hollow relief that came with self-denial. Sometimes, I would embrace humility and lock the door to temptation, choosing the path of restraint with a sense of weary relief. At other times, the pull of liberty and impulse would prove too strong, and I would yield, only to be met with regret. Ultimately, my choices were shaped by the immediate weight of memory and emotion—never by certainty, but always by the ceaseless struggle within.
